questions.explain: `p = &a` makes `p` point to `a`; `*p = 7` writes through the pointer, so `a` becomes 7.
option_notes: That was a's value before the assignment through the pointer.
`%d` prints the int value, not an address.

questions.prompt: An `int *p` holds the address 0x2000 and `sizeof(int)` is 4. What address does `p + 3` hold?
questions.explain: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the size of the pointed-to type: `p + 3` is 3 * 4 = 12 bytes further, 0x2000 + 0xC = 0x200C.
option_notes: Adding 18 is neither 3 nor 12; hex 12 is 0x0C.

questions.prompt: Which statement allocates room on the heap for a copy of the string "Hello"?
questions.explain: A string needs one extra byte for the terminating `'\0'`: 5 letters + 1 = 6 bytes. `char s[6]` is stack (not heap) memory and the literal is read-only static data.
option_notes: One byte short: the terminator would overflow the block.
That is an array on the stack, not heap memory.
That only points to a string literal; nothing is allocated.

questions.prompt: Given `struct point { int x, y; } a = {1, 2}, b;` what does `b = a;` do?
options: Makes b an alias of a
Copies every member of a into b
Does not compile: structs cannot be assigned
questions.explain: Structs are values in C: assignment copies all members. `b` is an independent copy; changing `b.x` afterwards does not affect `a`.
option_notes: C has no aliases; that would need a pointer.

questions.prompt: Which expressions are equivalent to `v[2]` for an array `v`?
questions.explain: `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`, and addition is commutative, so `*(2 + v)` and even `2[v]` work. `&v[2]` and `v + 2` are the ADDRESS of the element, not the element.
option_notes: Same thing with the operands swapped.
This is a pointer to v[2], not its value.
Also a pointer, not the value.

questions.prompt: Which statements about arrays and pointers are true?
options: `sizeof(arr)` for an array is the size of the whole array in bytes
`sizeof(ptr)` for a pointer is the size of an address
An array name can be re-assigned to point elsewhere
A pointer variable can be re-assigned to point elsewhere
questions.explain: The array name is not a modifiable variable: it always denotes the same block. A pointer is a variable and can point anywhere. `sizeof` on a pointer does not know how many elements it points to.
option_notes: True (when `arr` is the actual array, not a parameter).
False: you cannot assign to an array name.

questions.prompt: To access member `x` through a pointer `p` to a struct, write `p{{0}}x`.
`free` must receive a pointer that was returned by `malloc`, `calloc` or {{0}}.
questions.explain: Freeing anything else (a stack address, a pointer into the middle of a block, a pointer already freed) is undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: `calloc(n, size)` differs from `malloc` because it sets all the bytes it returns to {{0}}.
questions.explain: `malloc` leaves the memory uninitialised (garbage); `calloc` zero-fills it.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to grow a heap array safely.
items: Call realloc and keep the result in a temporary pointer
Check that the temporary pointer is not NULL
Assign the temporary pointer to the array pointer
questions.explain: If you wrote `v = realloc(v, n)` directly and it failed, `v` would become NULL and the old block would leak. Using a temporary keeps the original pointer valid on failure.

questions.prompt: Put these three lines in the right order to swap `*a` and `*b`.
questions.explain: Save one value first, overwrite it, then store the saved value in the other place. Any other order loses a value.
